item_name: Met Police LFR van deployments and their publication
operator: Metropolitan Police Service (MPS). Deployment locations are allocated by the Met's Central Tasking and Co-Ordination Group (CTCG), chaired by a Deputy Assistant Commissioner, and each operation is separately authorised by a senior authorising officer.
vendor: NEC (NeoFace) facial recognition software; cameras supplied by Axis Communications. Delivered from marked, MPS-liveried vans - the LFR Policy permits three delivery mechanisms: a static MPS-liveried vehicle, a secure MPS-liveried hoarding, or a limited series of networked CCTV cameras back to a central control point.
london_coverage_summary: Vehicle-mounted LFR is still the bulk of the Met's live facial recognition, and it has scaled sharply: 3 deployments in 2020, 23 in 2023, 180 in 2024 and 231 in 2025 - roughly one every 1.6 days. Every one of the 32 London boroughs has hosted at least one deployment since 2020, but the load is heavily uneven, with Westminster (75), Croydon (55) and Newham (35) far ahead. The Met publishes a detailed retrospective archive - a per-year PDF grid of every deployment with location, date, duration, watchlist size, alerts and arrests - but publishes nothing in advance: notice consists of signage put up on the day and a same-day post on the borough's X/Twitter account. There is no live or upcoming-deployment map or list, official or third-party.

camera_count_claimed: The Met does not claim a number of cameras for van deployments - it counts deployments, not cameras. Two dedicated LFR vans were stated in the MPS Live Facial Recognition Annual Report 2025 (published 31 October 2025): 'At present, LFR deployments are typically carried out twice a week using two dedicated vans.' The January 2026 policing White Paper promised 40 new LFR vans for town centres across England and Wales, taking the national fleet to about 50; Liberty records a fleet of 10 new facial recognition vans already enabling deployments in Bedford and Manchester. How many of those 50 are or will be Met vans has not been published. [uncertain]
fixed_vs_mobile: Mobile: effectively all of it. Of 231 deployments logged in 2025, all but the Croydon static-camera operations from 1 October 2025 onward (12 rows labelled 'North End, Croydon') were van-delivered - roughly 219 van deployments in 2025. Permanently installed: two street-furniture-mounted camera locations, both in Croydon, covered by the separate police_fixed item. The Met's stated direction of travel is to shift routine hotspot work off the vans and onto static cameras (West End and Soho by end-2026, London-wide from 2027) precisely because van availability caps how many simultaneous deployments are possible.
geographic_concentration: Since 2020, by borough: Westminster 75, Croydon 55, Newham 35, Southwark 23, Camden 20, Haringey 20, Greenwich 20, Hammersmith and Fulham 16, Barking and Dagenham 15, Lewisham 15, Wandsworth 15, Hackney 13, Brent 13, Havering 12, Waltham Forest 12, Redbridge 11, Hounslow 9, Ealing 9, Tower Hamlets 9, Lambeth 8, Kingston 6, Kensington and Chelsea 6, Enfield 5, Sutton 5, Islington 4, Harrow 3, Hillingdon 3, Bromley 3, Richmond 2, Merton 2, Bexley 2, Barnet 1. Within boroughs the pattern is high streets and transport interchanges: Powis Street Woolwich, Oxford Circus, Stratford Broadway, Wembley Central, Walthamstow Central, High Street North East Ham, Rye Lane Peckham, Kilburn High Road, Green Street Newham, Walworth Road, South Street Romford, Clarence Street Kingston, Dalston Kingsland, Bond Street station, Station Parade Barking and Leicester Square are the most repeated. 110 distinct location labels appear in the 2025 record alone. Zoe Garbett's audit found 263 deployments since 2020 in wards with a lower-than-London-average share of White residents against 180 in higher-than-average wards (145 to 86 in 2025).
last_confirmed_active_date: 2026-09-03 - LFR was deployed to crime hotspots in Westminster borough, announced the same day on the Met's Westminster X/Twitter account [uncertain: this rests on a search-result extract of the post, which could not be opened directly]. Firmer, fully sourced 2026 evidence: 12 August 2026, Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said the Met had arrested more than 2,000 people using LFR since the start of 2024, and Statewatch reported in June 2026 that the Met made about 1.7 million LFR scans in the first four months of 2026.
evidence_of_current_activity: (1) The Met's facial recognition page, as archived on 3 August 2026, lists a 'Live Facial Recognition - Deployment Record 2026' alongside the 2025, 2023-24 and 2020-22 records, so the force is still logging deployments this year. (2) Statewatch, June 2026: roughly 1.7 million faces scanned by the Met in the first four months of 2026. (3) Mid-May 2026: the Met used LFR at a protest for the first time, at the 'Unite the Kingdom' event in Camden. (4) 23 June 2026: Rowley announced an expansion of LFR, not a retreat. (5) 12 August 2026: Rowley's 2,000-arrests-since-2024 figure, reported by LBC. (6) Liberty's tracking records that the Met doubled its weekly LFR deployments in the year to July 2026. (7) A deployment in Westminster on 3 September 2026, three days before this research. Nothing suggests any pause.
known_pauses_or_withdrawals: No pause. There was a dormant year - zero deployments in 2021, during the pandemic - and a long pause after the 2016-2020 trials, but use has risen every year since 2022. Croydon Council and Islington Council passed motions opposing LFR in their boroughs and Assembly Member Zoe Garbett called in February 2026 for an immediate halt; none of this stopped deployments. The Met has not so far used LFR inside the boundaries of Notting Hill Carnival, confining cameras to the approaches - a self-imposed limit rather than a withdrawal. The judicial review dismissed on 21 April 2026 removed the most likely legal brake.
publication_channel: Retrospectively and in detail, on the Met's own facial recognition page: https://www.met.police.uk/police-forces/metropolitan-police/areas/about-us/about-the-met/facial-recognition-technology/ under the heading 'Deployment records'. Four per-period PDFs are published there - Deployment Record 2026, Deployment Record 2025, Deployment Record 2023 to 2024, and Deployment Record 2020 to 2022. Each row gives deployment location (street or landmark level, e.g. 'Powis St, Woolwich', 'Stratford B'way'), date, duration to the minute, LFR use case, watchlist size, minimum threshold setting, total alerts, true and false alerts confirmed and unconfirmed, false alert rate, arrests, other outcomes, no-action counts, and an estimate of faces seen. Direct PDF: https://www.met.police.uk/SysSiteAssets/media/downloads/force-content/met/advice/lfr/deployment-records/live-facial-recognition-deployment-record-2025.pdf . Prospectively, the only channel is a post on the relevant borough policing X/Twitter account on the day, plus physical signage placed before the zone of recognition. The Met also publishes an annual LFR report (2025 edition released 31 October 2025; the 2026 edition is expected around October 2026).
live_feed_or_map_available: No - and this is the clearest negative finding in this file. There is no live feed, no map and no forward-looking list of Met LFR van deployments anywhere, official or third-party. The Met's own LFR page carries only retrospective deployment-record PDFs; as captured on 3 August 2026 it contained no 'upcoming deployments' section, no map and no calendar. The Met's 2025 annual report describes the practice in its own words: when deploying to a new location officers engage with local communities and businesses, 'display signage on the day, and announce the deployment via social media'. That social media post is same-day, is scattered across borough accounts rather than aggregated, is not archived anywhere searchable, and is not machine-readable. Campaign groups have not filled the gap: Big Brother Watch and Liberty campaign against LFR and publish analysis, but neither runs a deployment tracker or map, and no crowdsourced live listing of Met LFR vans was found. The nearest thing to a map is Zoe Garbett's February 2026 static choropleth of deployments by borough since 2020, which is historical and borough-resolution only. In short: you can find out with considerable precision where an LFR van was after the fact, and essentially nothing about where it will be.
advance_notice_period: None. Signage goes up on the day and the social media announcement is same-day; the deployment record is published retrospectively, and the 2025 record was not complete until after year end. No Met policy document commits to any minimum advance notice - the LFR Policy requires only that signage be used before the zone of recognition. Community engagement with local businesses and, in one documented case, a place of worship does happen ahead of a new location, but that is private engagement, not public notice. [uncertain - no published figure exists to cite, so 'none' is inferred from the absence of any advance-publication commitment plus the Met's own 'on the day' description]
foi_or_audit_sources: The unchecked expansion of live facial recognition technology in London, Zoe Garbett AM, London Assembly, 10 February 2026 - the definitive independent audit, assembled from Mayor's Question Time answers and FOI; source of the per-year deployment counts, the per-borough table, the ward-level ethnicity analysis, the vendor identification and the finding that the Met refused to disclose officer-hours per deployment. London Assembly / Mayor's Question Time answers on london.gov.uk, including 'Live Facial Recognition (LFR) trial in Croydon' and the March 2025 analysis showing over half of 2024's 180 deployments fell in areas with a higher-than-average Black population - which also records that Garbett asked for more precise location data than borough level and did not get it. Statewatch, June 2026, reports the Met refused an FOI request for the full Croydon evaluation on the grounds it would appear in the October 2026 annual report. Big Brother Watch (whose director Silkie Carlo was second claimant in the 2026 judicial review) and Liberty publish running campaign analysis. The Met's own deployment records and annual report are the primary quantitative source and are unusually detailed for a UK police force.
legal_basis: No primary legislation. Common law policing powers, the Data Protection Act 2018 Part 3 for law enforcement processing of biometric data, the Human Rights Act 1998 and ECHR Articles 8, 10 and 11, the Surveillance Camera Code of Practice, and the Met's published LFR Policy, Legal Mandate, Data Protection Impact Assessment and Equality Impact Assessment. Permitted use cases are crime hotspots, missing person hotspots, protective security operations at critical national infrastructure and at events, and response to specific intelligence about a sought person's location. Each deployment needs a documented authorisation, a bespoke intelligence-led watchlist built from images already held (typically custody images, around 15,000-17,000 entries in the 2025 records) compiled no more than 24 hours in advance and deleted immediately afterwards, and a threshold setting - 0.64 throughout the published 2025 record. Non-matching faces are deleted immediately.
regulatory_challenges: Thompson and Carlo v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis: judicial review of the Met's 2024 LFR policy dismissed by the High Court on 21 April 2026, the court holding the policy had sufficient clarity, foreseeability and safeguards to meet the ECHR 'quality of law' test. Shaun Thompson had been wrongly stopped after being misidentified as his brother; Silkie Carlo of Big Brother Watch was second claimant; the Equality and Human Rights Commission intervened. Both claimants said they would appeal. The controlling precedent remains R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058. A Home Office consultation on a new legal framework for law enforcement biometrics ran 4 December 2025 to 12 February 2026; the May 2026 King's Speech promised a dedicated framework and legislation was expected in autumn 2026, but none had been laid at the time of writing - which is the substance of Big Brother Watch's complaint that the police are 'rushing ahead under their own rules'.
oversight_body: No LFR-specific statutory regulator. In practice the Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime (MOPAC), the London Assembly Police and Crime Committee, the Information Commissioner's Office, the London Policing Ethics Panel, and the residual functions of the Biometrics and Surveillance Camera Commissioner. Authorisation is internal to the Met (CTCG allocation plus a senior authorising officer, with NPCC-rank sign-off before deployment).
key_uncertainties: 1. The number of LFR vans the Met currently operates is not published. 'Two dedicated vans' is the Met's own figure in its October 2025 annual report, but the Met more than doubled weekly deployments over the following year, which two vans could not obviously absorb; the 40-van and 10-van figures in circulation are the Home Office's national fleet for England and Wales, not the Met's. Treat 'two' as a floor and out of date. 2. The 2026 deployment record could not be retrieved. It is listed on the Met's own page (Wayback capture, 3 August 2026) but the link carries no file extension; every direct request was blocked by Cloudflare or returned 404, and the Wayback Machine holds no copy. So there is no per-deployment 2026 location list in this file, and the 2026 borough distribution and deployment count are unknown. The per-borough totals given above are cumulative to February 2026. 3. The 3 September 2026 Westminster deployment rests on a search-result extract of a borough police X post that could not be opened directly - treat as strongly indicative rather than verified. 4. The cameras list is not a list of installations. Van deployments leave nothing behind; the entries are recurring deployment sites drawn from the Met's own 2025 record, and the site with the most 2025 deployments, North End Croydon, is the fixed-camera site belonging to the police_fixed item. camera_count_confirmed (17) is the number of sites enumerated here, not a count of hardware; 110 distinct location labels appear in the 2025 record alone and the full set is in the published PDFs. 5. No postcodes or coordinates are given because the Met publishes none - its location labels are street or landmark names ('Oxford Circus', 'Stratford B'way', 'Bond St Stn'), and the parking spot within that street is never recorded. Geocoding these would be an invention, not a finding. 6. The exact van parking positions, the hours a van will be present, and the wording and placement of signage are not published at all. 7. Statewatch's figure of roughly 1.7 million Met scans in the first four months of 2026 sits oddly against the arrest figures reported elsewhere and could not be cross-checked against the 2026 deployment record; it is cited as an order of magnitude, not a precise total.

sources.title: MPS LFR Deployments 2025 - Live Facial Recognition Deployment Record 2025 (PDF)
sources.what_it_supports: PRIMARY SOURCE and the backbone of this file. 231 deployment rows for 2025, each with location, date, duration, use case, watchlist size (roughly 14,900-16,900), threshold (0.64 throughout), alert breakdown, false alert rate, arrests, other outcomes and estimated faces seen. sources.title: Metropolitan Police - Facial Recognition Technology page (Wayback capture)
sources.what_it_supports: PRIMARY, both positively and negatively. Positively: the deployment archive exists and has four parts - Deployment Record 2026, 2025, 2023 to 2024, and 2020 to 2022. sources.title: MPS Live Facial Recognition Policy document
sources.date: 2024 policy, under annual review to March 2026
sources.what_it_supports: PRIMARY. The three permitted delivery mechanisms including the static MPS-liveried vehicle; the permitted use cases; watchlist construction and 24-hour rule; the eight-stage technical process; the signage requirement before the zone of recognition and the absence of any advance-publication duty. This is the policy the High Court upheld in April 2026.

sources.title: The unchecked expansion of live facial recognition technology in London - report by Zoe Garbett AM
sources.what_it_supports: Independent audit and the source of the borough table. Deployments by year (2020:3, 2021:0, 2022:6, 2023:23, 2024:180, 2025:231) and the deployment-every-N-days figures; total deployments and per-100,000 rates for all 32 boroughs; the 263-to-180 ward-ethnicity split; vendor identification (NEC software, Axis cameras); the January 2026 White Paper promise of 40 new LFR vans for England and Wales; the observation that the Met 'currently only has access to a small number of LFR vans'; and the point that fixed cameras remove the visual cue a van provides.

sources.title: Facial Recognition campaign page (Liberty)
sources.what_it_supports: That the Met doubled its number of weekly LFR deployments across London in the year to July 2026; a fleet of 10 new facial recognition vans enabling deployments in Bedford and Manchester; the June 2026 West End/Soho static announcement with London-wide rollout in 2027; and that the May 2026 King's Speech promised a legal framework that had not yet been laid before Parliament.

sources.title: England: Police use of facial recognition technology growing rapidly (Statewatch)
sources.what_it_supports: 2026 currency: approximately 1.7 million Met LFR scans in the first four months of 2026; the first known LFR deployment at a protest, mid-May 2026 at the 'Unite the Kingdom' event in Camden; 40 additional government-funded vans taking the England and Wales fleet to about 50; and the Met's refusal of an FOI for the Croydon evaluation pending its October 2026 annual report.
